desc:
Among all contiguous subarrays of nums that contain at least k elements, take the one with the largest average. Return that largest average rounded down to the nearest integer (round towards negative infinity, so the floor of -2.5 is -3).

Equivalently: return the largest integer x such that some subarray of length at least k has average at least x.

Example: nums = [1, 12, -5, -6, 50, 3], k = 4. The subarray [12, -5, -6, 50] has sum 51 over 4 elements, average 12.75, and it is the best one of length at least 4 (the other candidates average 0.5, 10.5, 10.4, 10.8 and about 9.17). The answer is 12.
hints: Checking all subarrays of length at least k costs O(n2) with prefix sums. Instead of finding the best average directly, ask a yes/no question about a guess.

Is there a subarray of length at least k whose average is at least x? Subtract x from every element: the question becomes whether some such subarray has a sum of at least 0. If the answer is yes for x it is also yes for every smaller value.

Binary search the integer x between min(nums) and max(nums). To test one x, build prefix sums of nums[i] - x and, while sweeping the right end i ≥ k, maintain the minimum prefix among positions 0..i-k; the test succeeds as soon as prefix[i] - minPrefix ≥ 0.
editorial: Maximising an average directly is awkward, but checking a guess is easy. A subarray of length L has average at least x exactly when the sum of (nums[i] - x) over it is at least 0. Call a guess feasible if such a subarray of length at least k exists. Lowering x raises every shifted sum, so feasibility is monotone: true for all small x, false for all large x. The answer is the last feasible integer.

To test a guess in O(n), let P be the prefix sums of the shifted values. A subarray ending at index i (prefix position i + 1) with length at least k starts at a prefix position at most i + 1 - k, so the best partner is the smallest prefix value seen so far at that distance. Sweep once, update the running minimum one step behind the current end, and stop successfully when the difference is non-negative.

Any average lies between min(nums) and max(nums), and x = min(nums) is always feasible, so the search range is at most 2·106 wide, about 21 probes. Total time is O(n log(max - min)) with O(1) extra space if the prefix sum is kept as a running value (the prefix array is also fine). Use the upper midpoint when moving lo = mid, and remember that Python's // already floors negative numbers correctly.
